idiom_name: parameterized base receiving the deriving type + compile-time hook calls
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: parameterize the shared base on the concrete type (or use a language facility that exposes the implementing type, such as a trait's Self), and have the base's interface operations call the concrete type's hooks through that parameter; because the base is instantiated only after the concrete type is complete, the calls resolve at compile time. State the required hook operations as a compile-time contract and let violations fail the build, keep the base free of runtime type information and of virtual dispatch, and restrict its construction so it cannot exist on its own. Where the language offers a direct way to name the implementing type (Rust's Self, Swift's protocol Self, recursive generic bounds), prefer that facility; CRTP is a C++ workaround for the absence of such a keyword.
code_sketch:
base<Concrete>:
    interface() -> concrete.hook()      # resolved at compile time
concrete : base<concrete>
    hook() -> ...
algorithm<B extends base<...>>(values)  # one instantiation per concrete type
pitfalls: Two concrete types claiming the same base instantiation (in languages that permit it, the base's downcast is then silently wrong).
Forgetting to restrict the base so that it cannot be instantiated or used on its own.
Assuming the mechanism is cheap everywhere: where generics are erased or instance dispatch stays virtual, the same structure buys typing only.

Wrong move: calling a derived hook from the CRTP base constructor or destructor -> the derived subobject does not yet exist or is already destroyed, so static_cast<Derived*>(this) is undefined behaviour where a virtual call would at worst be a defined pure-call failure -> instead defer the call to an explicit init() invoked after full construction.

Wrong move: storing CRTP siblings in one heterogeneous collection because they 'share a base' -> Base<A> and Base<B> are unrelated types with nothing in common -> instead add a separate virtual common base or use type erasure, or keep virtual dispatch.

Wrong move: renaming or re-signaturing a derived hook during refactoring -> with nothing virtual there is no override diagnostic, so the member is silently hidden and the base calls the wrong function or fails deep in instantiation -> instead give hooks a distinct prefix and constrain the contract with a C++20 concept or static_assert so violations are hard errors.
